# **Architectural Blueprint for a Web-Based 4D Drosophila Simulation (MaleCNS v1.0)**

## **Executive Summary**

This report defines the comprehensive architecture, mathematical formalisms, and implementation strategy for a fully browser-based, 4D computational simulation of the adult male *Drosophila melanogaster*. By integrating the complete MaleCNS v1.0 connectome—comprising 166,700 neurons—with the biologically constrained Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neural dynamics of the Shiu et al. (2024) model, this project yields a high-fidelity, closed-loop virtual organism running entirely on the client side1. The simulation leverages a WebGPU compute shader architecture to parallelize the propagation of a highly optimized 25.5-million-edge subset of the connectome, ensuring a strict 60 frames-per-second (FPS) performance budget without reliance on server-side compute pipelines5. Coupled with Three.js-based instanced rendering for real-time volumetric neural visualization, an articulated physical fly body, and first-person compound-eye visual processing, the final deliverable serves as a publicly accessible Hugging Face Space designed for both neurobiological exploration and interactive sandbox experimentation7.

## **Key Findings**

### **Connectome Data Pipeline and Preprocessing**

The foundation of the simulation rests on the Janelia MaleCNS v1.0 dataset, released globally under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license1. The full dataset contains granular information detailing synaptic partnerships, spatial somata locations, and predicted neurotransmitter profiles. To bridge the gap between static biological storage formats and a real-time WebGPU environment, a rigorous offline data preprocessing pipeline must be executed prior to deployment.  
The raw data is distributed via Google Storage buckets as Apache Arrow .feather files, providing high-speed columnar data storage suitable for out-of-core processing9. The preprocessing pipeline ingests three primary artifacts from the Janelia repository:

| File Name | Format | Size | Download URL |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| body-annotations-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather | Arrow IPC (.feather) | 14.5 MB | [https\://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/body-annotations-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather](https://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/body-annotations-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather) \[cite: 10, 11\] |
| body-neurotransmitters-male-cns-v1.0.feather | Arrow IPC (.feather) | 43.2 MB | [https\://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/body-neurotransmitters-male-cns-v1.0.feather](https://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/body-neurotransmitters-male-cns-v1.0.feather) \[cite: 10, 11\] |
| connectome-weights-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather | Arrow IPC (.feather) | 1.05 GB | [https\://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/connectome-weights-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather](https://storage.googleapis.com/flyem-male-cns/v1.0/connectome-data/flat-connectome/connectome-weights-male-cns-v1.0-minconf-0.5.feather) \[cite: 10, 11\] |

Loading a 151.8-million-edge graph into browser GPU memory (VRAM) exceeds the constraints of consumer hardware and standard WebGL/WebGPU buffer allocation limits. Research indicates that function-preserving sparsification of the connectome is highly dependent on both connection strength and specific behavioral tasks2. Consequently, the graph must be aggressively pruned to a retained subset of 25.5 million directed edges. This is achieved by implementing a minimum synapse weight threshold—typically preserving connections containing ![][image1] synapses—while explicitly safeguarding the sparse pathways targeting descending motor neurons to ensure the retention of functional sensorimotor loops11.  
For optimal parallelization in WGSL compute shaders, the pruned graph is transformed into the Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format14. This serialization strategy mathematically flattens the two-dimensional connectivity matrix into three tightly packed, contiguous binary buffers. The row\_ptrs array, encoded as 32-bit unsigned integers (Uint32Array), maps the 166,700 neuron indices to their starting position in the column array. The col\_indices array, also a Uint32Array, contains the 25.5 million downstream target neuron identifiers. Finally, the weights array, encoded as 32-bit floating-point numbers (Float32Array), contains the signed synaptic strengths. These buffers are concatenated into a lightweight binary artifact, allowing rapid client-side network transmission and direct zero-copy mapping into WebGPU StorageBuffers without incurring JavaScript garbage collection overhead16.

### **Computational LIF Simulation Model**

The simulation executes a mathematically rigorous phenomenological model. Shiu et al. (2024) developed a network-scale Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model originally utilizing the Python-based Brian2 simulator2. To translate this framework into a highly concurrent WebGPU environment, the governing continuous differential equations must be discretized using the Euler method for rapid parallel computation over a discrete time step ![][image2].  
The membrane potential ![][image3] for each neuron ![][image4] is governed by a first-order differential equation. The potential is perpetually drawn toward a resting state, modified by incoming synaptic currents, and perturbed by simulated biological noise. The continuous equation is defined as:  
![][image5]  
Where ![][image6] is the resting potential, ![][image7] represents the aggregate incoming synaptic currents, and ![][image8] introduces additive membrane noise simulating spontaneous network activity via unit white noise ![][image9]2. When ![][image3] exceeds the spike threshold ![][image10], a discrete spike is emitted, the potential is reset, and the neuron enters a refractory period ![][image11].  
Synaptic polarity within this differential system is strictly dictated by the consensus neurotransmitter prediction of the presynaptic neuron9. Excitatory responses are driven primarily by Acetylcholine (ACh), whereas inhibition is driven by Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)20. Crucially, the Shiu et al. (2024) model asserts that Glutamate operates as an inhibitory neurotransmitter within these specific *Drosophila* sensorimotor circuits, a convention that must be algorithmically enforced during the CSR weight compilation22.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value / Formulation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Resting Potential | ![][image6] | ![][image12] mV13 |
| Spike Threshold | ![][image10] | ![][image13] mV3 |
| Integration Step | ![][image2] | ![][image14] ms2 |
| Noise Amplitude | ![][image15] | ![][image16] or ![][image17] mV (for active states); ![][image18] mV (silent)2 |
| Synaptic Weight | ![][image19] | ![][image20], where magnitude equals physical synapse count2 |
| Membrane Time Const. | ![][image21] | ⚠️ Parameter not explicitly stated; typically ![][image22] ms inferred from Brian2 defaults. |
| Synaptic Time Const. | ![][image23] | ⚠️ Parameter not explicitly stated; inferred from instantaneous current injection models. |
| Synaptic Delay | ![][image24] | ⚠️ Parameter not explicitly stated; presumed ![][image18] or minimal network propagation delay. |
| Refractory Period | ![][image11] | ⚠️ Parameter not explicitly stated; inferred as ![][image25] ms in secondary simulation ports16. |

Optogenetic activation or direct sensory stimulation is modeled as an independent Poisson drive applied to targeted sensory populations2. Stimulated sensory neurons receive a continuous mathematical stream of Poisson-distributed spikes. The synaptic weight of this external artificial stimulus is fixed at ![][image26], delivered at a specified frequency rate ![][image27], allowing the simulation of environmental interactions such as odor plumes or mechanical deflection2.

### **Descending Motor Mapping and Sensorimotor Behavior**

To achieve an "embodied" virtual fly, the raw spiking activity of the 166,700 simulated neurons must continuously map onto physical behaviors. The central brain communicates with the Ventral Nerve Cord (VNC) via Descending Neurons (DNs)25. The simulation isolates key functional pathways validated by the connectome to drive an animation state machine.  
Visual information processing relies heavily on Visual Projection Neurons, specifically the LC4 and LC9 populations. These neurons serve as primary feature detectors for looming stimuli, representing approaching predators or obstacles. The LC9 pathways provide robust, high-bandwidth inputs for directional takeoff and escape sequences7. Consequently, rapid increases in LC9 spike rates trigger the state machine's transition from an idle or walking state directly into the flight state.  
Turning behavior is strictly modulated by the activation of specific descending command populations, notably DNa02 and DNa117. Differential spiking rates between the left-hemisphere and right-hemisphere DNa02 populations dictate the continuous yaw torque applied to the virtual fly's physical body. Backward walking and complex postural steering are governed by the MDN (DNp50) cluster25.  
The rendering engine incorporates a hierarchical animation state machine that interpolates between distinct kinematics states: Walk, Turn, Fly, and Land7. The WebGPU pipeline writes the aggregated, exponentially smoothed spike rates of these specific DN clusters into a dedicated readback buffer. A JavaScript controller polls this buffer asynchronously and blends the fly's skeletal animation weights—derived from high-resolution biological rigging models—ensuring fluid, biologically plausible motor transitions11.

### **Rendering and Virtual Environment Architecture**

Displaying a highly dense biological network at 60 FPS while concurrently managing physical environment logic requires specialized rendering paradigms, precluding the use of individual DOM elements or standard polygonal meshes for every neuron.  
The simulation utilizes Three.js or Babylon.js InstancedMesh architectures to achieve neural volumetric rendering7. A single spherical geometry is instanced 166,700 times within the graphics pipeline. A custom GLSL or WGSL vertex shader references a WebGPU texture or StorageBuffer containing the instantaneous membrane potential (![][image28]) of every neuron. The shader interpolates an emissive colormap mapped strictly to the ![][image29] voltage domain, creating a pulsating, real-time visualization of network activity7.  
The fly's morphology is rendered using physically based rendering (PBR) materials mapped to a detailed *Drosophila* exoskeleton. The environmental neuropil volumes—such as the Mushroom Body and Optic Lobes—are rendered as transparent, depth-tested boundary meshes to provide anatomical context around the instanced neuron cloud9. *Drosophila* beat their wings at approximately 200 Hz. Because standard monitor refresh rates (60-144 Hz) cause severe temporal aliasing, wing motion is rendered using shader-based motion blur. This technique procedurally spreads the wing geometry over its stroke arc relative to the global flight state, bypassing the need for computationally expensive sub-frame temporal sampling7.  
The first-person camera operates via spatial raycasting through the compound eye's hexagonal facet geometry. Each of the \~892 retinotopic ommatidia per eye maps pixel luminance changes from the Three.js scene into the initial sensory neurons (e.g., Lamina monopolar cells L1/L2), effectively closing the visuomotor loop8. Furthermore, a core interactive feature allows users to "paint" stimuli directly onto the brain volume. Using GPU picking and depth-plane cross-sections, user mouse inputs cast a volumetric cylinder into the 3D space. Neurons intersecting this brush radius are flagged in an auxiliary WebGPU buffer, forcing their voltage to the ![][image10] threshold and triggering the Poisson sensory drive equations to simulate optogenetic activation7.

### **WebGPU WGSL Compute Shader Architecture**

WebGPU is strictly required over legacy WebGL 2.0 to access native compute shaders (WGSL) and the robust StorageBuffer read/write capabilities necessary for executing the LIF algorithm efficiently on the client GPU6.  
The simulation utilizes a highly optimized two-pass dispatchWorkgroups architecture to prevent race conditions during synaptic propagation. The pipeline guarantees that a full integration step and subsequent matrix multiplication resolve within a strict performance budget, allowing the 166,700 neurons and 25.5 million edges to be processed in under 3 milliseconds on consumer hardware6.

Code snippet  
// WebGPU WGSL Pseudocode for LIF Update Loop  
@group(0) @binding(0) var\<storage, read\_write\> voltages: array\<f32\>;  
@group(0) @binding(1) var\<storage, read\_write\> spikes: array\<u32\>;  
@group(0) @binding(2) var\<storage, read\_write\> currents: array\<f32\>;  
@group(0) @binding(3) var\<storage, read\> row\_ptrs: array\<u32\>;  
@group(0) @binding(4) var\<storage, read\> col\_indices: array\<u32\>;  
@group(0) @binding(5) var\<storage, read\> weights: array\<f32\>;

// Pass 1: Leaky Integrate and Fire  
@compute @workgroup\_size(256)  
fn integrate\_pass(@builtin(global\_invocation\_id) global\_id: vec3\<u32\>) {  
    let i \= global\_id.x;  
    if (i \>= 166700u) { return; }  
      
    let v\_rest \= \-52.0;  
    let v\_th \= \-45.0;  
    let dt\_tau \= 0.01; // dt / tau\_m approximation  
      
    // Euler integration of LIF equation  
    var v \= voltages\[i\];  
    v \= v \+ ((v\_rest \- v) \* dt\_tau) \+ currents\[i\];  
      
    // Evaluate threshold and emit spike  
    if (v \>= v\_th) {  
        spikes\[i\] \= 1u;  
        voltages\[i\] \= v\_rest; // Reset  
    } else {  
        spikes\[i\] \= 0u;  
        voltages\[i\] \= v;  
    }  
      
    // Clear current buffer for the next frame  
    currents\[i\] \= 0.0;  
}

// Pass 2: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) Propagation  
@compute @workgroup\_size(256)  
fn propagate\_pass(@builtin(global\_invocation\_id) global\_id: vec3\<u32\>) {  
    let i \= global\_id.x;  
    if (i \>= 166700u) { return; }  
      
    // Only propagate if the presynaptic neuron spiked  
    if (spikes\[i\] \== 1u) {  
        let start\_edge \= row\_ptrs\[i\];  
        let end\_edge \= row\_ptrs\[i \+ 1u\];  
          
        for (var e \= start\_edge; e \< end\_edge; e \= e \+ 1u) {  
            let target\_idx \= col\_indices\[e\];  
            let w \= weights\[e\];  
            // Atomic add required in production WGSL to prevent race conditions   
            // from concurrent presynaptic neurons hitting the same target  
            atomicAdd(\&currents\_atomic\[target\_idx\], w);  
        }  
    }  
}

The data flow within the GPU follows a strict synchronization barrier between these two passes.

| Stage | Input Buffers | Process | Output Buffers | Sync Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Stage 1** | voltages, currents | LIF Euler Integration | voltages (updated), spikes | Threads operate independently. No atomic locks required. |
| **Barrier** | N/A | workgroupBarrier() | N/A | Execution halts until Stage 1 completes for all neurons. |
| **Stage 2** | spikes, row\_ptrs, col\_indices, weights | SpMV Graph Traversal | currents (accumulated) | Requires atomic addition on the output buffer due to scatter-write concurrency. |
| **Stage 3** | voltages, spikes | Readback Polling | DN\_motor\_state | Async buffer mapping to JavaScript for animation interpolation. |

### **Implementation Phases**

The deployment of the virtual organism is divided into six distinct agile phases. Each phase establishes foundational architecture required for the subsequent milestone, governed by definitive acceptance criteria.

| Phase | Milestone | Acceptance Criteria |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 1** | **Data Preparation & Serialization** | 151.8M edges algorithmically pruned to 25.5M. Graph serialized into binary CSR format (row\_ptrs, col\_indices, weights). Metadata mapping neuron IDs to 3D spatial coordinates verified against neuroglancer volumes. |
| **Phase 2** | **WebGPU Kernel Parity** | WGSL LIF simulator deployed locally. Resulting membrane potentials and spike cascades are cross-validated against the original Brian2 Python reference implementation for deterministic stimulus inputs. |
| **Phase 3** | **Instanced 3D Rendering** | Three.js integration complete. 166.7K spheres rendered simultaneously at ![][image30] FPS. Custom fragment shader dynamically maps live WebGPU voltage states to emissive colors without CPU bottlenecking. |
| **Phase 4** | **Motor Mapping & Articulation** | LC4/LC9 and DNa02 outputs successfully parsed into a JavaScript controller. Fly skeleton transitions smoothly between walk, turn, and fly animations in direct mathematical response to descending neural activity. |
| **Phase 5** | **Closed-Loop & Sandbox** | First-person hexagonal vision implemented. Raycast painting enables manual targeted stimulation. Multi-fly instancing manages spatial states accurately without ![][image31] collision physics degradation. |
| **Phase 6** | **Hugging Face Deployment** | Full stack bundled with Vite/Webpack. Asynchronous chunk loading implemented for .scx weight artifacts. Application serves securely via HTTPS on Hugging Face Spaces. |

## **Risks & Low-Confidence Data**

To ensure scientific accuracy and platform stability, several technical, biological, and theoretical risks must be mitigated prior to final deployment on a public facing server.  
⚠️ **Unspecified LIF Parameters:** While Shiu et al. (2024) provide explicit values for the resting potential (![][image6]), threshold (![][image10]), and noise scaling (![][image15]), several critical temporal parameters are absent from the immediate publication text. The exact values for the membrane time constant (![][image21]), synaptic time constant (![][image23]), synaptic delay (![][image24]), and absolute refractory period (![][image11]) are frequently inferred from Brian2 framework defaults or broader literature2. For example, refractory periods are sometimes assumed as ![][image25] ms in secondary simulation ports16. Furthermore, the exact Poisson spike rate (![][image27]) for sensory classes other than sugar-evoked responses is not universally parameterized in the open repository2. These parameters must be explicitly set, documented as assumptions, and ideally exposed in the application's user interface for interactive tuning.  
⚠️ **3D Soma Coordinates Derivation:** The connectome tables provide raw synaptic locations (x, y, z in 8nm units) and complex skeletons, but highly accurate singular volumetric coordinates (somata) for all 166,700 neurons are not guaranteed9. Certain orphan segments or projection neurons may contain missing or NaN coordinate values if directly parsing the feather tables31. The renderer must implement a mathematical fallback to calculate the spatial centroid of a neuron's point cloud derived from the neuroglancer precomputed volume, or gracefully hide somaless neurons from the 3D visual layer without removing them from the underlying WGSL compute graph9.  
⚠️ **WebGPU Browser Compatibility:** The simulation is highly dependent on WebGPU. While natively supported on Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge) and Safari, Firefox support remains largely constrained behind developer flags6. Attempting a pure JavaScript/CPU fallback utilizing a WebWorker pool is excessively slow for processing 25.5 million edges iteratively16. The application architecture must include an initial capability check upon loading; if navigator.gpu is unavailable, it must prompt users with a Safari/Chromium fallback strategy rather than attempting to execute a failing WebGL state machine.  
⚠️ **Edge Pruning Functional Impact:** The aggressive pruning of the connectome from 151.8 million to 25.5 million edges represents an approximate 83% reduction in graph density. Because random or purely magnitude-based pruning can cause catastrophic "functional cliffs" in signal propagation, there is a risk that this subset severs delicate sensorimotor pathways2. The algorithmic retention threshold must be carefully weighted to protect sparse Descending Neuron (DN) command channels that might otherwise be discarded under a strict uniform synapse-count cutoff.  
⚠️ **Licensing Ambiguity:** Deployment on a public platform like Hugging Face requires strict adherence to open-source licensing. The Janelia MaleCNS v1.0 dataset operates under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), permitting open reuse, modification, and redistribution provided proper scientific credit is attributed2. Conversely, the Shiu et al. (2024) reference code is distributed via the MIT License22. A comprehensive LICENSE and CREDITS overlay must be packaged directly inside the application bundle, explicitly segregating the data attribution from the codebase license, and citing the respective nature papers before the Hugging Face Space goes public4.
